title: Sam's Barbershop: preparing the year-end trial balance, its purpose, and errors it cannot detect
participant_role: Accountant hired by Sam's Barbershop to prepare and explain a trial balance from the owner's year-end account balances
judge_role: Owner of Sam's Barbershop, the only stylist, who knows little about accounting and wants the records set up correctly
scenario:
You are to assume the role of an accountant for SAM'S BARBERSHOP. The owner of the business (judge) wants you to explain and prepare a trial balance.

The owner of SAM'S BARBERSHOP (judge) is passionate about cutting and styling hair and is excited about the opportunity to own a business. Currently, the owner (judge) is the only stylist at the business but hopes to grow and wants to make sure that the accounting records are set up correctly. The owner (judge) knows very little about managing the accounts of a business so has hired you to help. The owner (judge) has done a good job of keeping track of the balances of the accounts. The year-end account balances are below:

[Year-end account balances: see exhibits]

You will use this information to prepare a trial balance which will help you check for errors. You will then meet with the owner (judge) to:
- Prepare a trial balance
- Explain the purpose of the trial balance
- Discuss what errors cannot be detected from the trial balance

You will present the information to the owner (judge) in a role-play to take place in the owner's (judge's) office. The owner (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented the information and have answered the owner's (judge's) questions, the owner (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

judge_questions: Why do we need accurate accounting before hiring other employees?
Why do some expense costs change and some stay the same?

solution.overview: A strong answer sorts the 15 accounts into debit balances (assets, drawings, expenses) and credit balances (liabilities, capital, revenue), showing both columns total $53,450, and explains where the trial balance sits in the accounting cycle. The presenter explains that the trial balance proves debits equal credits and is the base for the financial statements, then points out the errors it cannot catch: posting to the wrong account, a wrong amount in a balanced entry, and unrecorded transactions.

answer: List accounts in ledger order: assets, liabilities, owner's equity, drawings, revenue, expenses

Debit balances: Cash 19,175; Supplies 1,625; Prepaid Insurance 2,100; Prepaid Rent 2,300; Accounts Receivable 1,050; Equipment 3,100; Owner's Drawings 4,110; Rent Expense 8,470; Supplies Expense 680; Advertising Expense 970; Insurance Expense 5,570; Utilities Expense 4,300
Credit balances: Accounts Payable 4,900; Owner's Capital 21,450; Service Revenue 27,100
Total debits 53,450 = total credits 53,450, so the ledger is in balance
This is the unadjusted trial balance as of December 31; adjusting entries (for example, using up prepaid rent and insurance and counting supplies) come next in the cycle
It checks that total debits equal total credits, because every journal entry posted must have equal debits and credits
It is a summary of every general ledger account balance at one date
It is the starting point for adjusting entries and for preparing the income statement, statement of owner's equity and balance sheet
It will not balance if a journal entry had unequal debits and credits or if a posting error was made to the ledger
Accounting cycle: analyze transactions, journalize, post to the ledger, prepare the trial balance, adjust, prepare statements, close

by_task.task: Errors the trial balance cannot detect
answer: Posting to the wrong account (for example, a haircut supply charged to Equipment instead of Supplies)
Posting the wrong amount on both sides of a balanced journal entry
Unrecorded transactions: a sale or bill never entered leaves both columns equally short
Also an entry recorded twice, or compensating errors that offset each other
So a balanced trial balance is necessary but not proof that the books are correct; source documents and account reviews are still needed

calculations.label: Total credits
steps: Accounts Payable 4,900 + Owner's Capital 21,450 + Service Revenue 27,100 = 53,450

calculations.label: Net income for the year (model answer, useful context for the owner)
calculations.result: Net income 7,110 before any adjusting entries

judge_question_answers.question: Why do we need accurate accounting before hiring other employees?
answer: You need to know the shop can afford a second stylist: current net income is about $7,110 and cash is $19,175, so the numbers show what wage or commission is realistic
Payroll adds new accounts (Wages Expense, Payroll Tax Expense, payroll liabilities) that must be recorded and filed with the government correctly
Accurate records let you measure how much revenue each stylist brings in versus what they cost
Clean books are also needed if you seek a loan or a lease for a bigger space to house more employees

judge_question_answers.question: Why do some expense costs change and some stay the same?
answer: Fixed costs, such as rent ($8,470) and insurance ($5,570), stay the same each month regardless of how many haircuts you give
Variable costs, such as supplies (shampoo, razors, capes) and some utilities, rise and fall with the number of customers
Some costs are mixed, like utilities with a base charge plus usage, or advertising which you can raise or cut by choice
Knowing which costs are fixed helps set a price per haircut that covers them; variable costs tell you the cost of each extra customer

key_concepts.definition: A list of every general ledger account and its balance at one date, with debit balances in one column and credit balances in the other. Total debits must equal total credits.

The steps repeated each period: analyze transactions, journalize, post to the ledger, prepare an unadjusted trial balance, record adjusting entries, prepare an adjusted trial balance and financial statements, and close the temporary accounts.
The side on which an account increases. Assets, drawings and expenses have debit normal balances; liabilities, owner's capital and revenue have credit normal balances.
Every transaction is recorded with equal debits and credits, which is why the trial balance should balance.
The collection of all accounts and their running balances; the trial balance summarizes it.
The unadjusted trial balance is prepared before adjusting entries (prepaid rent, insurance, supplies used, depreciation); the adjusted trial balance is prepared after and is used for the statements.

key_concepts.term: Errors a trial balance cannot detect
key_concepts.definition: Posting to the wrong account, using the wrong amount on both sides of an entry, omitting a transaction entirely, recording an entry twice, or errors that offset each other.
Writing 1,625 as 1,265 (transposition) or 162.50 (slide) on one side only; the resulting difference is divisible by 9, a quick clue when a trial balance does not balance.
An asset for something paid in advance, such as prepaid rent or insurance; it becomes an expense through an adjusting entry as it is used up.
Money the owner takes from the business for personal use; a debit-balance equity account closed to Owner's Capital at year end.
Fixed costs (rent, insurance) stay the same in total regardless of activity; variable costs (supplies) change in total with the number of customers served.
Owners use accurate records to decide on hiring, pricing and expansion, to file taxes and to obtain loans.
